sections.title: Feedforward Neural Networks — Layers, Notation and Parameters

blocks.html: Start here A feedforward neural network is just many sigmoid-type neurons arranged in layers, where information flows one way: from the input, through hidden layers, to the output. This page fixes the notation (aᵢ, hᵢ, Wᵢ, bᵢ) that the whole of backpropagation uses — learn it well and the rest becomes much easier.

sections.title: Output Functions and Loss Functions — Linear, Softmax, Squared Error, Cross-Entropy

blocks.html: Start here What the network should output depends on the question. Predicting a rating (a real number) needs a different last layer and a different loss than picking one fruit out of four. This page gives the two standard pairs you will use again and again: linear + squared error and softmax + cross-entropy.
blocks.text:
Start here What the network should output depends on
the question. Predicting a rating (a real number) needs
a different last layer and a different loss than picking one
fruit out of four . This page gives the two standard pairs you
will use again and again: linear + squared error and softmax + cross-entropy .

1. Case 1: predicting real
numbers

sections.title: Backpropagation — the Idea, and Gradients at the Output Layer

blocks.html: Start here The network made a mistake. Who is to blame? Backpropagation answers this by passing the blame backwards, layer by layer, using the chain rule. This page builds the intuition and then derives the first and most famous result: at a softmax + cross-entropy output, the gradient is simply ŷ − (true label).
blocks.text:
Start here The network made a mistake. Who
is to blame? Backpropagation answers this by passing the blame
backwards, layer by layer, using the chain rule. This page builds the
intuition and then derives the first and most famous result: at a
softmax + cross-entropy output, the gradient is simply ŷ − (true
label) .
1. Focus on one weight

blocks.html: To learn W₁₁₂ (one weight in the first layer) with gradient descent we need ∂L(θ)/∂W₁₁₂. How does a weight deep inside the network affect the loss at the top?
blocks.text:
To learn W₁₁₂ (one weight in the first layer) with gradient descent
we need ∂L(θ)/∂W₁₁₂ . How does a weight deep inside the
network affect the loss at the top?

2. Easy case: a deep but thin
network

blocks.html: Imagine a network with one neuron per layer: x₁ → a₁₁ → h₁₁ → a₂₁ → h₂₁ → a_L1 → ŷ → L(θ).

a₁₁ → h₁₁ → a₂₁ → h₂₁ → a_L1 → ŷ → L(θ).

3. The blame story (intuition)

blocks.alt: The loss blames the output layer, which points to the weights and the hidden layer below, and so on down to the first layer
blocks.caption:
Blame flows downward through the layers — that is
backpropagation.

blocks.html:
1. We get a loss −log ŷ_ℓ at the output. Who is responsible?
  2. We tell the output layer: “You are not producing the right output — take responsibility.”
  3. The output layer says: “I take my share, but I am only as good as the hidden layer and weights below me” — after all, ŷ = O(W_L h_{L−1} + b_L).
  4. We ask W_L, b_L and h_L what’s wrong. W_L and b_L take full responsibility. h_L says: “I’m only as good as my pre-activation layer.”
  5. The pre-activation says: “I’m only as good as the hidden layer and weights below me.”
  6. Continue down… the responsibility lies with all the weights and biases.

The story in 5 lines

blocks.html:
1. A feedforward network computes aₖ = bₖ + Wₖhₖ₋₁ and hₖ = g(aₖ) for each hidden layer, then ŷ = O(a_L).
  2. Parameters θ = all Wₖ and bₖ; learned by gradient descent, θ ← θ − η∇θ.
  3. Real-valued outputs → linear output + squared error. Classes → softmax + cross-entropy (L = −log ŷ_ℓ).
  4. Backpropagation passes blame from the loss down through the layers using the chain rule.
  5. With softmax + cross-entropy, the output gradient is just ŷ − e(ℓ).

Common traps

blocks.html:
• ∇ŷ L (only one non-zero entry, −1/ŷ_ℓ) is not the same as ∇a_L L (ŷ − e(ℓ), all entries non-zero).
  • Use Wᵀ (transpose) when passing gradients down.
  • ⊙ is element-wise, not a matrix product.
  • Sigmoid output can’t predict values outside (0, 1) → use linear for real values.
  • The entries of ŷ − e(ℓ) always add to 0.
  • Slide erratum: one slide writes ∇W_L ∈ ℝ^(n×k); it should be k × n, the same as W_L.
